steps.prompt: In a survey, $30$ of $50$ students like sport. If you pick one student at random, how likely are they to like sport? What changes if you only pick from students who also like music?

cards.title: Probability
cards.body: Probability $=$ favourable outcomes $\div$ all equally likely outcomes, a number from $0$ to $1$. $P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$. For independent events, multiply: $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$.

cards.title: Reading a two-way table
cards.text: A survey of $80$ students: of the $50$ who play a sport, $20$ also play an instrument; of the $30$ who don’t play a sport, $12$ play an instrument. So $32$ students play an instrument in all, and $48$ don’t.
cards.note: A two-way table puts sport / no sport in the rows and instrument / no instrument in the columns, with the totals at the ends.

cards.title: Worked example: "given" picks the group
cards.problem: In the survey of $80$ students, $50$ play a sport ($20$ of them play an instrument) and $30$ don’t ($12$ of them play an instrument). A student who plays an instrument is picked at random. What is the probability they play a sport?

steps.text: "Picked from the instrument players" means only they count.
Not $\frac{20}{80}$ and not $\frac{20}{50}$: divide by the group you pick from.

cards.title: Expected counts
cards.body: If an outcome has probability $p$ and you repeat the experiment $n$ times, expect about $np$ of them. Out of $600$ rolls of a fair die, expect about $100$ sixes.

prompts: How do you decide which total to divide by in a two-way table question?
